issues.subcategory: results contradicted in discussion
issues.description: The Discussion section claims that 'results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness.' However, in the Results of Primary Analysis 1, anxiety was explicitly non-significant (χ²=3.62, p=.306), and the Results text itself states 'No significant effects by episode type emerged for more general emotional content...or other specific emotions/constructs (i.e., anxiety, anger, death).' The Discussion therefore misrepresents the actual statistical findings by adding anxiety as a differentiator that was never observed.
issues.quote: In terms of overall mean differences, few reliable differences emerged though results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness.

issues.subcategory: beta coefficient sign direction inconsistent with described effect direction
issues.description: In Table 3, all three interaction betas for anger × time are negative (−0.023, −0.026, −0.027), yet the text claims 'anger increased more steeply during attempt episodes compared to all other episode types.' Similarly, for self-focus, the betas are negative (−0.015, −0.010) while the text states 'self-focus tended to increase preceding an attempt.' For positive emotion, betas are positive (+0.010, +0.027, +0.016) while the text states 'positive emotion decreased more steeply during attempt episodes.' These sign inconsistencies suggest either the reference category coding is reversed from what is described, the time variable direction is opposite to what is stated, or there are reporting errors in the direction of effects. Without knowing the precise model parameterization, interpreting whether effects are increases or decreases is impossible.
issues.quote: There was also a significant interaction for anger words, such that anger increased more steeply during attempt compared to all other episode types, including ideation (z=2.00, p=.046), depressed (z=2.49, p=.013), and positive (z=2.54, p=.0111) episodes (Figure 1C).

issues.subcategory: asymmetric time-anchoring of episode types
issues.description: Attempt episodes are systematically defined as the two-week window immediately preceding a discrete behavioral endpoint (the attempt), creating a time-locked epoch anchored to an outcome event. By contrast, ideation, depressed, and positive mood episodes are free-floating two-week periods with no equivalent terminal anchor. This structural asymmetry confounds the comparison: any psychological pattern that naturally intensifies toward any salient event would appear to differentiate attempt episodes from the others purely by design. The slope analyses are particularly vulnerable—the attempt window by construction captures an escalation trajectory leading to an event, whereas other windows have no such inherent directional structure.
issues.quote: past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the two-week period prior to the attempt as a 'suicide attempt episode'; 2) two-week episodes of suicide ideation (not resulting in a suicide attempt); 3) two-week episodes of depressed mood or high stress (not resulting in suicide ideation or attempt); and 4) two-week episode of positive mood

issues.subcategory: severe episode-level missing data with systematic bias
issues.description: Only 134 of 293 collected episodes (46%) contained any SMS data, meaning 54% of episodes provided no data. More critically, only 15 of 33 participants had SMS data from at least one suicide attempt episode—the central comparison condition of the study. The remaining 12 participants with any data contributed exclusively to non-attempt episode comparisons. This means the primary within-subjects comparison (attempt vs. other episodes) is effectively based on a subset of 15 participants, yet the stated N is 33. The authors acknowledge this but claim mixed-effects models 'handle missing data,' which addresses statistical estimation but does not resolve the underlying selection bias: participants lacking attempt SMS data may differ systematically (e.g., older attempts, phone changes, encryption use) in ways related to the constructs studied.
issues.quote: Among these 27 participants, 15 had data from at least one reported suicide attempt; the other 12 participants contributed data from non-suicide attempt episodes and were still included in the analyses.

issues.subcategory: within-subjects design structurally compromised
issues.description: The study is described throughout as a within-subjects design, which is presented as a key methodological strength over between-subjects comparisons. However, 12 of the 27 participants with any SMS data contributed only to non-attempt episode analyses. The attempt vs. other episode comparison therefore necessarily includes a between-subjects component—participants who provided attempt data versus those who did not. Individual differences in personality, phone usage patterns, communication style, and psychiatric severity could confound comparisons between episode types when the same individuals do not contribute to all conditions.
issues.quote: the other 12 participants contributed data from non-suicide attempt episodes and were still included in the analyses.

issues.subcategory: post-hoc data-driven window selection
issues.description: The two-week analysis window is presented initially as a theoretically justified a priori decision, but then the Methods reveals it was additionally validated by visual inspection of the data: 'The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures to identify when the rate of change appeared to be most pronounced.' The visual inspection found 'changes tended to occur most notably and often around 7 days prior to the suicide attempt,' which contradicts using a 14-day window. Selecting or confirming the analysis window based on the data and then analyzing with that window is circular and inflates Type I error. The 14-day choice also appears inconsistent with the empirical finding of 7-day change.
issues.quote: The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures to identify when the rate of change appeared to be most pronounced. Specifically, temporal visualizations, using a smoother (loess) function, were constructed for each variable of interest...changes tended to occur most notably and often around 7 days prior to the suicide attempt.

issues.subcategory: multiple testing without correction in small underpowered sample
issues.description: The authors ran approximately 25 or more statistical tests across two sets of analyses and explicitly declined to apply multiple comparisons corrections, citing Rothman (1990). The justification is internally contradictory: they simultaneously argue the study is underpowered and therefore prone to Type II error, while relying on an uncorrected alpha to report significant findings. With ~25 independent tests at α=.05, approximately one to two false positives would be expected by chance alone. Several reported significant p-values are marginal (anger interaction: p=.049; ideation × time for positive emotion: p=.049), making these particularly suspect without correction. The Rothman (1990) citation applies primarily to epidemiological contexts with pre-specified hypotheses; here, many analyses were explicitly exploratory.
issues.quote: our analyses involved running a fairly large number of tests, which potentially increases the chances of rejecting the null hypothesis due to the sheer number of tests. Given this is a pilot study with a small and already potentially underpowered sample and the fact that we did not have concrete directional hypotheses for many of the tests, we decided not to artificially suppress Type I error (i.e., using a multiple comparisons correction)

issues.subcategory: absence of pre-registration
issues.description: The study has no pre-registration, despite combining confirmatory hypotheses (self-focus, negative sentiment, social disengagement were predicted a priori) with extensively exploratory analyses. Without pre-registration, it is impossible to distinguish hypotheses that were genuinely specified in advance from those generated post-hoc after inspecting the data. The authors acknowledge exploration but do not formally separate confirmatory from exploratory results. The OSF materials (cited as containing screening surveys) do not appear to include a registered analysis plan. This is especially problematic given the study involves numerous researcher degrees of freedom: choice of LIWC variables, time window selection, model specification, and handling of non-convergence.
issues.quote: Numerous aspects of this research were exploratory by nature. Given the lack of prior research examining when one might expect any differences to emerge prior to a suicide attempt, we did not have hypotheses on whether language differences would be observed for episodes overall (means) but not changes over time (slopes), or vice versa.

issues.subcategory: significant omnibus with no significant pairwise comparisons
issues.description: For death words in Analysis 2, the authors report a significant omnibus chi-square interaction (χ²(3)=9.47, p=.024) but then state 'there were no significant differences in change over time for attempt compared to all other episodes (zs=0.33-1.83, ps=.067-.739).' A significant omnibus interaction with 4 levels implies that at least one pairwise contrast should be significant. If all attempt-comparison pairwise tests are non-significant, the omnibus significance must be driven by differences among non-attempt episodes (e.g., ideation vs. positive mood). This is confirmed when the authors note 'ideation episodes appeared to show a steeper decrease in death words compared to both attempt and positive mood episodes.' The significant omnibus result is therefore not evidence that death word trajectories are unusual near suicide attempts—directly contradicting the inference that this finding is relevant to identifying attempt episodes.
issues.quote: There was also a significant interaction for death words, χ²(3)=9.47, p=.024. However, there were no significant differences in change over time for attempt compared to all other episodes (zs=0.33-1.83, ps=.067-.739)

issues.subcategory: causal and predictive claims from retrospective correlational data
issues.description: Throughout the manuscript, particularly in the Clinical Implications section, the authors make strong causal and predictive claims that substantially exceed what the retrospective, correlational, cross-sectional design can support. The study identifies associations between episode type (classified retrospectively) and language features in historical text messages. It cannot establish that these patterns would prospectively predict future suicide attempts in a new sample. Claims about developing 'an objective monitoring tool capable of tracking individuals' communication behind the scenes, notifying suicidal individuals and/or their clinician' far outstrip the inferential basis of a pilot correlation study.
issues.quote: Knowledge gained from this study could put us one step closer to the development of an objective monitoring tool capable of tracking individuals' communication 'behind the scenes,' notifying suicidal individuals and/or their clinician or family if their patterns of communication indicate increasing levels of suicide risk.

issues.subcategory: absence of non-attempter control comparison
issues.description: The study includes only suicide attempters and compares different episode types within this group. There is no non-clinical control group and no group of individuals who have never attempted suicide. Without such a comparison, it is impossible to determine whether the observed language patterns (e.g., increased anger before attempt) are specific to suicide attempters or whether they characterize any individual experiencing a period of acute distress or escalating emotional state. The patterns observed may reflect universal stress responses rather than markers specific to suicide risk.
issues.quote: By recruiting only individuals with a history of acting on their suicidal thoughts (i.e., actual suicide attempts), or on the cusp of acting on their thoughts (i.e., aborted or interrupted suicide attempts), this study focused on those behaviors most strongly associated with and predictive of suicide completion.

issues.subcategory: LIWC applied to individual short text messages
issues.description: LIWC was developed and validated for use on documents of substantial length (essays, interviews, social media posts). The current study applies it to individual SMS text messages, which may contain only a handful of words (the average message length is not reported). When a message contains 5–10 words, a single word can produce LIWC percentages of 10–20%, making scores extremely unreliable and highly variable. While the authors convert percentages to counts and model them as proportions, the fundamental problem remains: very short texts generate unstable LIWC estimates with low validity. The authors do not assess or report the mean word count per message across episode types, which is critical for evaluating LIWC reliability.
issues.quote: Each individual SMS message was inputted into and scored using the 2015 version of Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC)...The majority of LIWC variables calculate scores based on the percentage of words belonging to a given category

issues.subcategory: social engagement operationalization does not match interpersonal theory constructs
issues.description: The interpersonal theory of suicide (Joiner, 2005; Van Orden et al., 2010) specifies two distinct constructs: thwarted belongingness (feeling disconnected from others) and perceived burdensomeness (feeling like a burden). The study operationalizes social engagement as the ratio of sent to received text messages and counts of outgoing/incoming messages. Message frequency and direction do not constitute valid operationalizations of either thwarted belongingness or perceived burdensomeness—a person could send many messages while feeling profoundly disconnected, or could feel burdened without reducing outgoing communication. The operationalization is also atheoretical with respect to which direction changes should occur: the hypothesized decrease in outgoing messages is not clearly derivable from the theory.
issues.quote: we tested whether suicide attempters demonstrated greater signs of disengagement from and burdensomeness on their social support networks prior to suicide attempts compared to other episodes by examining patterns in outgoing vs. incoming messages.

issues.subcategory: highly non-representative sample limits generalizability
issues.description: The sample is 84.8% female, 60.6% Caucasian, mean age 20.4 years, 94% with 'some college' education, and recruited from a university participant pool. This demographic profile is highly unrepresentative of the broader population of suicide attempters. Suicide attempt rates and methods, communication patterns, and text messaging behavior differ substantially by gender, age, education, and race/ethnicity. Males are four times more likely to die by suicide yet represent only ~15% of the sample. The paper acknowledges the gender-completion discrepancy in limitations but does not adequately flag that these demographic features may fundamentally alter the generalizability of all findings—including the specific language features identified.
issues.quote: Most of the participants were female, White, and college-aged.

issues.subcategory: retrospective findings overclaimed as real-time biomarkers
issues.description: The abstract, title, and conclusion repeatedly describe the findings as enabling 'real-time' risk detection and as 'real-time digital markers of suicide risk.' However, the entire study is retrospective: participants retrospectively identified past episodes and the text messages from those episodes were analyzed after the fact. No aspect of the study demonstrates that these patterns would be detectable in real time or that a prospective, real-time monitoring system would show similar performance. The gap between 'patterns found in historical data' and 'real-time risk detection' is enormous and not bridged by any analysis in the study.
issues.quote: Results suggest private electronic communication has the potential to provide real-time digital markers of suicide risk.

issues.subcategory: retrospective episode classification and date uncertainty
issues.description: The entire study depends on participants accurately recalling the dates of past suicide attempts and other episodes, potentially years after the fact. 'Somewhat certain' responses (meaning dates 'may be off by a few days') were counted as acceptable, yet this uncertainty is substantial for a 14-day analysis window—a 3-day offset shifts 21% of the window to the wrong period. The authors correctly note that communication data are not retrospective, but the episode labels applied to those data are, and label misclassification (e.g., misassigning attempt-period messages to ideation periods) would directly attenuate and distort the primary effect estimates in unpredictable ways.
issues.quote: Participants were generally confident about the accuracy of the dates they selected, rating 90.3% of episodes as 'very certain' (i.e., exact days) or 'somewhat certain' (i.e., may be off by a few days).

issues.subcategory: study characterized as prospective when fundamentally retrospective
issues.description: The authors explicitly claim 'we utilized a prospective research design' to justify the study's inferential validity over truly cross-sectional work. This characterization is misleading. A prospective design requires participants to be enrolled before the outcome occurs and followed forward in time. This study enrolls participants who have already experienced attempts, retrospectively classifies past periods, and retrospectively analyzes pre-existing communication data. While the text messages were generated before the attempt (and thus prospectively in a trivial sense), the scientific design—hypothesis generation, participant selection, episode identification, data analysis—is entirely retrospective. This mislabeling inflates the perceived strength of causal inference.
issues.quote: By reconstructing the timeline of recent suicidal behaviors through a retrospective clinical interview, we utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt, overcoming the power issues of a 'true' prospective study design.

issues.subcategory: platform-dependent systematic exclusion of data
issues.description: A systematic, platform-based form of data loss is inadequately addressed: 'a number of iPhone users had encryption settings on their phones that prevented third-party iPhone software from accessing text data.' iPhone users with encryption enabled are systematically excluded from having their data collected. If iPhone vs. Android ownership correlates with demographics, privacy behaviors, or socioeconomic status—all plausible—this creates non-random missingness directly related to participant characteristics. The proportion of iPhone users excluded due to encryption is not reported, nor is any analysis of whether participants with vs. without accessible data differed on key variables.
issues.quote: a number of iPhone users had encryption settings on their phones that prevented third-party iPhone software from accessing text data.

issues.subcategory: random effects convergence failures inadequately described
issues.description: The Methods state that a maximal random effects model was planned, including random slopes for episode type, day, and their interaction by participant. The authors then note 'Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, only a by-participant slope of episode type was included in the final model.' This is a significant deviation from the stated analytic plan, but it is not reported which specific random slopes were dropped, whether different models were tested, or whether the simplification was applied identically across all outcome variables. Non-convergence can indicate model misspecification beyond just overfitting, and the consequences for inference depend on which slopes were dropped.
issues.quote: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, only a by-participant slope of episode type was included in the final model.

issues.subcategory: intraclass correlations and model fit statistics not reported
issues.description: Despite using multilevel mixed-effects models with three levels of nesting (participant, episode, message), no intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) are reported at any level. ICCs would characterize the degree of clustering and justify the multilevel approach. Similarly, no model fit statistics (AIC, BIC, or likelihood values for null models) are reported, making it impossible to evaluate absolute model quality or the adequacy of the random effects structure. The paper claims mixed-effects models produce 'more accurate and generalizable population estimates' but provides no empirical basis to evaluate this claim in the context of this specific dataset.
issues.quote: Advantages of mixed-effects models. A mixed-effects method was selected because of its well-established advantages in terms of producing more accurate effect estimates and its ability to handle missing data, non-normal outcome data, and unbalanced classes

issues.subcategory: power analysis assumptions inconsistent with achieved sample
issues.description: The power analysis states the study was designed around '30 suicide attempters (representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect).' However, the Results section reveals only 15 of 33 participants had SMS data from at least one suicide attempt episode—not 20 as the power analysis assumed. The power analysis was therefore too optimistic by 25% for the most critical comparison condition. The study was even more underpowered than the already-noted limitations acknowledge, further reducing confidence in non-significant findings and inflating concerns about false positives among the significant ones.
issues.quote: We determined that a sample size of 30 suicide attempters (representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect) would provide enough power to detect only large effect sizes

issues.subcategory: iatrogenic change sign ambiguity in Table 1
issues.description: Table 1 reports the iatrogenic change in 'Desire to die (0-10)' as 0.20 (positive, implying an increase from pre to post session). However, the Results text reports 'desire to die from pre (M=0.82, SD=1.10) to post (M=0.61, SD=0.90) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033.' The correct change score is −0.21 (a decrease). The positive value in Table 1 is therefore either a sign error or represents an absolute magnitude without direction, creating a potentially misleading impression that suicidal ideation increased during the study session. The t-test statistic and p-value indicate a significant decrease, consistent with the text but not the table value.
issues.quote: Iatrogenic – change pre to post | Desire to die (0-10) | 0.20

issues.subcategory: first-person pronoun use as self-focus in conversational SMS
issues.description: The operationalization of 'self-focus' as singular first-person pronoun frequency assumes that grammatical self-reference in text messages reflects the psychological construct of self-focused attention as described by Baumeister's escape theory. In natural SMS conversation, 'I' is used for mundane coordination ('I'm running late,' 'I can meet at 5') without implying any pathological self-focus. Prior research demonstrating first-person pronoun effects used poetry or clinical interviews, which are very different genres from transactional private messaging. The construct validity of this measure for everyday conversational SMS is not established and may introduce substantial construct-irrelevant variance.
issues.quote: In the current study, we tested whether use of first-person pronouns (as an indicator of self-focus) was greater prior to suicide attempts

issues.subcategory: log-odds betas reported as effect sizes without interpretive benchmarks
issues.description: The Methods state 'β (standardized values of the model parameter estimates in log odds units) are reported and serve as effect sizes.' Log-odds coefficients from GLMM models are not standardized effect sizes in the conventional sense, and the term 'standardized' is used incorrectly here—these are unstandardized regression coefficients on the log-odds scale. Without baseline rates for each LIWC category, readers cannot convert these to odds ratios or interpret their practical significance. The small magnitude of betas (e.g., 0.010 for positive emotion × time interaction) appears trivial without context, and no benchmarks for what constitutes a meaningful effect size in log-odds units for LIWC proportions are provided.
issues.quote: Mixed-effects models do not yield straightforward effect size statistics like other regression models (e.g., R2) and there is not a consensus on the most appropriate approach to take...Here, β (standardized values of the model parameter estimates in log odds units) are reported and serve as effect sizes.

issues.subcategory: robustness analyses in supplement not summarized
issues.description: The Methods describe 'Additional analyses...performed to examine the same set of outcome variables but in different ways to examine the robustness of the primary results and to see if the pattern of results changed' (Supplement 3), but these analyses are not described or summarized in the main text. Robustness analyses are scientifically important—if conclusions change with alternate analytic specifications, this fundamentally affects interpretation. Relegating these analyses to a supplement without any mention of their findings constitutes incomplete reporting and raises concerns that divergent results are being de-emphasized.
issues.quote: Condition comparisons using alternate data subsets. Additional analyses were performed to examine the same set of outcome variables but in different ways to examine the robustness of the primary results and to see if the pattern of results changed. Those analyses are available in Supplement 3 online.

issues.subcategory: typographical error in reported p-value
issues.description: A p-value is reported as '.0111' with four decimal digits rather than the standard three. The value 'p=.0111' should presumably be 'p=.011.' While apparently a typographical error, it introduces a numeric inconsistency in the reporting of statistical results that should have been caught during proofreading and reflects insufficient attention to numerical accuracy in the Results section.
issues.quote: positive (z=2.54, p=.0111) episodes (Figure 1C)

issues.subcategory: LIWC negation blindness acknowledged but implications not addressed
issues.description: The authors acknowledge in the Discussion that 'examining single words in isolation can fail to capture the semantic context of the word (e.g., "not happy" would count as "positive emotion" because negation is not accounted for).' This is a known and significant limitation of LIWC that could systematically bias all sentiment measures. However, this limitation is presented only as a future direction rather than as an active threat to the validity of the current results. In text messages, negation constructions ('not happy,' 'don't want to,' 'can't wait') are common and could introduce systematic misclassification that differentially affects different episode types, potentially producing artifactual differences or masking real ones.
issues.quote: One weakness of this approach is that examining single words in isolation can fail to capture the semantic context of the word (e.g., 'not happy' would count as 'positive emotion' because negation is not accounted for)
